etymology: Hebrew Yotsadaq (H3136), the LORD is righteous — from Yah, the covenant name, and tsadaq (H6663), to be righteous, to be just; the fuller form is Jehozadak.
biblical_def: Jozadak, also written Jehozadak, was the high priest's son who went into captivity when Nebuchadnezzar carried Judah away, and the father of Jeshua the high priest who came back. He himself never ministered in a standing temple: the house was burned before his turn came, and he died in Babylon. His son is named again and again in the record of the return — Jeshua the son of Jozadak raising the altar, beginning the house, and standing under Haggai's preaching (Ezr 3:8; 5:2; 10:18; Neh 12:26). The name means the LORD is righteous, and a man bearing it watched the sanctuary he was born to serve go up in smoke for his nation's sin. That is the confession Scripture puts in the mouth of the exiles themselves. The LORD is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment (Lam 1:18); O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces (Dan 9:7). Judah did not go into Babylon protesting her innocence. She went confessing that the God who judged her had done right, and the priestly line carried that verdict in its very name across seventy years until a son of Jozadak stood again at an altar in Jerusalem.
webster_summary: Son of Seraiah the high priest, carried into Babylon; father of Jeshua the high priest of the return. His name means the LORD is righteous.
webster_full: JOZADAK, Hebrew Yotsadaq, the LORD is righteous; also written Jehozadak.
Of the high-priestly line of Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas.
He went into captivity when the LORD carried away Judah by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.
Father of Jeshua, the high priest who returned with Zerubbabel.
Named repeatedly in Ezra and Nehemiah in the phrase Jeshua the son of Jozadak.
scriptures: Now in the second year of their coming unto the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, began Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the remnant of their brethren the priests and the Levites, and all they that were come out of the captivity unto Jerusalem; and appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to set forward the work of the house of the LORD.
Then rose up Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and began to build the house of God which is at Jerusalem: and with them were the prophets of God helping them.
And among the sons of the priests there were found that had taken strange wives: namely, of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren; Maaseiah, and Eliezer, and Jarib, and Gedaliah.
These were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest, the scribe.
corruption_summary: The exile is read as a political misfortune; Scripture presents it as the righteous judgment of God, confessed as such by the exiles themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: It is common to explain the Babylonian captivity purely in the terms of ancient geopolitics — a small kingdom caught between empires, destroyed by the ordinary machinery of conquest, its religious literature written afterward to make theological sense of a defeat. The prophets who lived through it will not have it. They had said for a century what would come and why: because ye have not heard my words, behold, I will send and take all the families of the north… and will bring them against this land (Jer 25:8-9). Nebuchadnezzar was the instrument; the hand was the LORD's, and the cause was covenant treachery.

What makes the exilic confession remarkable is that the victims agreed with the verdict. Daniel, who had done nothing to deserve Babylon, prayed O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces (Dan 9:7) and numbered himself with the guilty. That is repentance as Scripture defines it: not the admission that things went badly, but the confession that God was right. The principle to recover is that a people who can say the LORD is righteous over their own ruin are the only people positioned to be restored, because they have stopped disputing the diagnosis.

Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — righteousness, rightness; the LORD our righteousness (Jer 23:6).
Hebrew Yehotsadaq (H3087) — the fuller form of the name, used in 1 Chronicles 6:14-15 and in Haggai and Zechariah.
Greek dikaios (G1342) — just, righteous; that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus (Rom 3:26).
usage: “Jeshua the son of Jozadak” — the phrase that carries his memory.
“The LORD is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment” (Lam 1:18).
“Then rose up Zerubbabel… and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and began to build the house of God”.

etymology: Hebrew Yoyarib (H3114), the LORD contends or the LORD will plead — from Yah, the covenant name, and rib (H7378), to contend, to plead a cause at law; the fuller form is Jehoiarib.
biblical_def: Joiarib is the name of a priestly house and of more than one man in the restoration records. The house is the oldest of the priestly courses: when David divided the sons of Aaron into twenty-four orders, the first lot came forth to Jehoiarib (1Ch 24:7), and that course kept its precedence through the exile and the return, its men listed among the priests who dwelt at Jerusalem and came up with Zerubbabel (Neh 11:10; 12:6). Ezra also names a Joiarib among the chief men he sent to Casiphia to fetch Levites for the house of God (Ezr 8:16). The name is a courtroom word: the LORD contends. Rib is the verb of a legal dispute, and the prophets use it constantly for God's controversy with His people — the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land (Hos 4:1); Hear ye now what the LORD saith; Arise, contend thou before the mountains (Mic 6:1). It is also the verb of God contending on behalf of His people: he shall throughly plead their cause (Jer 50:34). The first course of the priesthood carried a name that says God does not leave matters unsettled.
webster_summary: The first of the twenty-four priestly courses appointed by David, and the name of men among the priests of the return. It means the LORD contends.
webster_full: JOIARIB, Hebrew Yoyarib, the LORD contends, or the LORD will plead; fuller form Jehoiarib.
The first lot of the twenty-four courses into which David divided the priests.
The house is named among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel.
A Joiarib is named among the chief men Ezra sent to fetch Levites for the house of God.
From rib, to contend or plead a cause at law.
scriptures: Now the first lot came forth to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah,
Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin.
Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name: he shall throughly plead their cause, that he may give rest to the land, and disquiet the inhabitants of Babylon.
corruption_summary: God's controversy with sin is recast as divine disappointment; rib is a legal action with a verdict at the end of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Preaching that has lost its nerve speaks of God being grieved, saddened, or disappointed by sin, and stops there. Scripture's own word is heavier. Rib is what a plaintiff does: he brings a suit, summons witnesses, states the charge and presses for judgment. When Micah says the LORD hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel (Mic 6:2), he is describing a trial, with the mountains called as witnesses. Sin is not a disappointment to be absorbed; it is a case to be answered.

The mercy in the doctrine is that the same verb describes God taking up the cause of the helpless. Their Redeemer is mighty; he shall throughly plead their cause (Jer 50:34); plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me (Psa 35:1). The identical action that condemns the impenitent defends the covenant people, because in Christ the suit against them has been answered and the Advocate now pleads for them — if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1Jn 2:1). The principle to recover is that the God who contends is the God who settles things, and that is good news for everyone who has taken His side against himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yoyarib (H3114), from Yah, the covenant name, and rib (H7378), to contend, to plead a legal cause.
roots_lines: Hebrew rib (H7378) — to contend, strive, plead a cause at law; the prophets' word for God's controversy with Israel.

Hebrew rib as noun (H7379) — a controversy, a suit; the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land (Hos 4:1).
Hebrew machaloqeth (H4256) — a division, a course; the twenty-four orders of the priesthood.
Greek parakletos (G3875) — advocate, one called alongside to plead; we have an advocate with the Father (1Jn 2:1).

“Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin”.

etymology: Hebrew Yoyada (H3111), the LORD knows — from Yah, the covenant name, and yada (H3045), to know. Not to be confused with Jehoiada the priest who crowned Joash four centuries earlier.
biblical_def: Joiada was a high priest of the restoration period, fourth in the line that runs from the return — Jeshua begat Joiakim, Joiakim also begat Eliashib, and Eliashib begat Joiada (Neh 12:10) — and himself the father of Jonathan and grandfather of Jaddua (Neh 12:11, 22). He is a different man from Jehoiada the priest who hid the infant Joash and crowned him king in Athaliah's day; the names are near cousins and the centuries between them are many. Joiada's own record is short and painful. Nehemiah closes his memoir with it: one of the sons of Joiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, was son in law to Sanballat the Horonite: therefore I chased him from me (Neh 13:28). The highest house in Israel had married into the family of the man who had done most to stop the wall from being built. Nehemiah's response was not negotiation but expulsion, and he asked God to remember the offenders because they have defiled the priesthood, and the covenant of the priesthood, and of the Levites (Neh 13:29). The lesson stands where Nehemiah put it, at the very end of the Old Testament's historical record: the last thing Israel is shown doing is compromising at the top.
webster_summary: A high priest of the restoration, son of Eliashib and father of Jonathan; one of his sons married a daughter of Sanballat and was driven out by Nehemiah.
webster_full: JOIADA, Hebrew Yoyada, the LORD knows.
A high priest of the period after the return from Babylon.
Son of Eliashib the high priest, and grandson of Joiakim.
Father of Jonathan, and grandfather of Jaddua.
Distinct from Jehoiada the priest who crowned Joash king of Judah.
scriptures: And Jeshua begat Joiakim, Joiakim also begat Eliashib, and Eliashib begat Joiada,
And Joiada begat Jonathan, and Jonathan begat Jaddua.
And one of the sons of Joiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, was son in law to Sanballat the Horonite: therefore I chased him from me.
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
corruption_summary: Separation is dismissed as tribalism; Nehemiah treats intermarriage with the covenant's open enemies as defilement of the priesthood itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 13 is an embarrassment to a church that has made inclusion its first virtue. A governor chases a high priest's grandson out of the city for a marriage, and calls the match a defilement of the covenant of the priesthood. Read as ethnic prejudice it is indefensible; read as Scripture writes it, the issue is never blood. Ruth the Moabitess is in the line of David; Rahab the Canaanite is in the genealogy of Christ. What Nehemiah opposed was a marriage alliance with Sanballat the Horonite, the standing adversary of the work of God, contracted at the summit of the priesthood — a union of the LORD's house with the LORD's enemies.

The principle carries straight into the New Testament, where it is put positively and personally: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers (2Co 6:14), and marriage is only in the Lord (1Co 7:39). This is not a rule about race or culture but about covenant loyalty, and it presses hardest on leaders, because a bishop then must be blameless… one that ruleth well his own house (1Ti 3:2-4). The principle to recover is that compromise entering at the top of a church does not stay at the top; Nehemiah acted as he did because he had seen what a generation of it produced the last time.

Hebrew chatan (H2860) — a son in law, a bridegroom; the relation Nehemiah broke up.
Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be unequally yoked; be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers (2Co 6:14).

“And Joiada begat Jonathan, and Jonathan begat Jaddua”.

etymology: Hebrew Yoyaqim (H3113), the LORD raises up — from Yah, the covenant name, and qum (H6965), to rise, to stand, to be established. Not to be confused with Jehoiakim king of Judah, who burned Jeremiah's scroll.
biblical_def: Joiakim was high priest in the generation after the return, son of Jeshua and grandson of Jozadak, and father of Eliashib (Neh 12:10, 12, 26). His days are used by Nehemiah as a marker for dating the registers of priests and Levites: in the days of Joiakim were priests, the chief of the fathers, and then follows the roll of the houses (Neh 12:12). He is a quiet figure, and his significance lies in where he stands — between the generation that built the altar and the generation of Nehemiah's wall, holding the office through the long middle years when nothing dramatic happened and the work could easily have been let go. His name says what those years were: the LORD raises up. Careful readers must keep him apart from Jehoiakim king of Judah, the man who cut Jeremiah's roll with a penknife and cast it into the fire on the hearth (Jer 36:23), of whom it was said that he should be buried with the burial of an ass. The names are almost the same and the men could not be more different: one burned the word of God, the other kept the house of God through an uneventful generation.
webster_summary: High priest of the generation after the return, son of Jeshua and father of Eliashib; his name means the LORD raises up.
webster_full: JOIAKIM, Hebrew Yoyaqim, the LORD raises up, or the LORD establishes.
High priest in the generation after the return from Babylon.
Son of Jeshua, grandson of Jozadak; father of Eliashib.
The registers of the priests and Levites were taken in his days.
Distinct from Jehoiakim king of Judah, who burned the roll of Jeremiah.
scriptures: And Jeshua begat Joiakim, Joiakim also begat Eliashib, and Eliashib begat Joiada,
And in the days of Joiakim were priests, the chief of the fathers: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah;
These were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest, the scribe.

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God ordinarily raises up His work through undramatic generations of plain faithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Joiakim has attracted no revisionist interest. The pressure he exerts is on a church addicted to moments. We tell the story of the restoration by its peaks — the altar raised in Ezra 3, the foundation laid with shouting and weeping, Nehemiah's wall in fifty and two days — and we pass over the decades in between, which is where Joiakim lived and served.

Scripture's own doctrine of the work is steadier than our appetite for it. Who hath despised the day of small things? asked Zechariah of that very generation (Zec 4:10), and the answer to the whole discouragement was Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts (Zec 4:6). The name Joiakim — the LORD raises up — states the agency. The principle to recover is that faithfulness through an uneventful decade is not a lesser form of service than leadership in a famous one; it is the ordinary means by which what was begun is still standing when the famous generation arrives.

etymology: Hebrew Chashshub (H2815), considerate or thoughtful — from chashab (H2803), to think, to devise, to reckon, to impute; the verb behind it was counted unto him for righteousness.
biblical_def: Hashub is the name of several men in the records of the restoration, most of them builders. One repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall with Malchijah the son of Harim, including the tower of the furnaces (Neh 3:11); another, named with Benjamin, repaired over against their house (Neh 3:23); a Hashub sealed the covenant of Nehemiah 10 (Neh 10:23); and Hasshub of the sons of Merari is named in the Levitical genealogy as an ancestor of Shemaiah, a Levite dwelling at Jerusalem (Neh 11:15; 1Ch 9:14). The detail in Nehemiah 3:23 is the one worth dwelling on: they repaired the wall over against their house. Nehemiah's method was to set each family to the stretch of wall nearest its own door, so that a man's labour and a man's stake stood in the same place. The name means considerate, from chashab, to think and to reckon — a good name for a builder, since a wall is what happens when somebody has thought it through. Scripture uses the same verb for God's reckoning: Abraham believed, and he counted it to him for righteousness (Gen 15:6).
webster_summary: The name of several men of the restoration, builders on the wall of Jerusalem and sealers of the covenant. It means considerate or thoughtful.
webster_full: HASHUB, Hebrew Chashshub, considerate, thoughtful; also written Hasshub.
1. A builder who repaired a piece of the wall and the tower of the furnaces.
2. One who with Benjamin repaired the wall over against their own house.
3. One of those who sealed the covenant in the days of Nehemiah.
4. Hasshub of the sons of Merari, in the Levitical genealogy at Jerusalem.
scriptures: Malchijah the son of Harim, and Hashub the son of Pahathmoab, repaired the other piece, and the tower of the furnaces.
After him repaired Benjamin and Hashub over against their house. After him repaired Azariah the son of Maaseiah the son of Ananiah by his house.
Also of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hashub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Bunni;
And of the Levites; Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Nehemiah's: a man builds best on the stretch of wall nearest his own door.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hashub is contested by nobody. What his verse contests is a modern habit of moral attention: the tendency to care intensely about distant causes while the nearest duties go undone. It has never been easier to be exercised about a wall a thousand miles away and to leave one's own gate off its hinges.

Nehemiah's arrangement was deliberate. Families repaired the wall in front of their own houses, which meant that the quality of the work and the safety of the family were the same question, and no man could do a careless job at somebody else's expense. Scripture orders duty the same way throughout: if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel (1Ti 5:8), and as we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, specially unto them who are of the household of faith (Gal 6:10). The principle to recover is that nearness creates obligation, and that the section of wall over against your own house is the one God has given you to build.

etymology: Hebrew Chenadad (H2582), commonly read as favour of Hadad — from chen (H2580), grace or favour, joined to Hadad, the name of a Syrian storm-god; a name whose second element is a relic of the nations among whom Israel had lived.
biblical_def: Henadad was the head of a Levitical house at the return from Babylon. His sons stood with Jeshua and Kadmiel to set forward the workmen in the house of God when the temple foundation was laid (Ezr 3:9); Bavai the son of Henadad, ruler of half of Keilah, repaired a portion of Jerusalem's wall, and Binnui the son of Henadad another piece from the house of Azariah to the corner (Neh 3:18, 24); and Binnui sealed Nehemiah's covenant among the Levites (Neh 10:9). The house appears at every stage of the rebuilding — foundation, wall, covenant — which is more than can be said of many with better names. And the name is the difficulty. Its second element is Hadad, a Syrian storm-god, a piece of the surrounding paganism lodged in the family of a Levite. Scripture reports it without comment, as it reports Mordecai (whose name echoes Marduk) and Esther (whose name echoes Ishtar). The exile left marks on the people who came out of it, and God did not require them to erase the marks before He would use them. He put them to work on His house.
webster_summary: Head of a Levitical house at the return from Babylon, whose sons oversaw the temple work and repaired the wall of Jerusalem.
webster_full: HENADAD, Hebrew Chenadad, commonly read favour of Hadad.
The head of a family of Levites who returned from the captivity.
His sons set forward the workmen in the house of God at the laying of the foundation.
Bavai his son, ruler of the half part of Keilah, repaired a piece of the wall.
Binnui his son repaired another piece and sealed the covenant with Nehemiah.
scriptures: Then stood Jeshua with his sons and his brethren, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together, to set forward the workmen in the house of God: the sons of Henadad, with their sons and their brethren the Levites.
After him repaired their brethren, Bavai the son of Henadad, the ruler of the half part of Keilah.
After him repaired Binnui the son of Henadad another piece, from the house of Azariah unto the turning of the wall, even unto the corner.
And the Levites: both Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel;
corruption_summary: A pagan element in a Levite's name is taken as proof that Israel's religion was syncretistic; Scripture reports the scar of exile without endorsing it.
corruption_paragraphs: Names like Henadad, Mordecai and Esther are regularly produced as evidence that the religion of Israel was simply one more strand of Near Eastern polytheism, its boundaries invented later by editors with an agenda. The inference outruns the evidence. A name is not a creed. Judah came out of seventy years in a land saturated with Bel and Nebo and Marduk, and it came out with the language, the calendar months and some of the personal names of that land stuck to it — and with a hatred of idols it had not possessed when it went in. That is the historical fact the theory cannot accommodate: the exile did not make Judah syncretistic, it cured her of the idolatry the prophets had denounced for centuries.

The pastoral use is plainer. The sons of Henadad were not told to change their father's name before they could carry timber for the house of God. Conversion does not require a man to erase his history; it requires him to serve a new Master with whatever he has, and the marks of where he came from often stay on him for life. Such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified (1Co 6:11). The principle to recover is that God builds His house with people who still carry the accent of the far country.

“Bavai the son of Henadad, the ruler of the half part of Keilah”.

etymology: Hebrew Azgad (H5803), commonly read strong is Gad or Gad is mighty — from az (H5794), strong, fierce, and the element Gad (H1409), which means a troop or fortune and was also the name of a heathen deity of fortune.
biblical_def: Azgad heads one of the lay families of the return from Babylon. The register in Ezra counts the children of Azgad, a thousand two hundred twenty and two (Ezr 2:12); Nehemiah's parallel register gives two thousand three hundred twenty and two (Neh 7:17); a second company came up later with Ezra himself — of the sons of Azgad; Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him an hundred and ten males (Ezr 8:12); and the house sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:15). Two things are worth naming. First, the family came back in waves: over a thousand with Zerubbabel, another hundred and ten with Ezra a generation later. Coming home from exile was not one decision made once by everybody; some returned at the first opportunity and some only after decades of hearing about it. Second, the difference between Ezra's figure and Nehemiah's for the same house is a reminder that the two registers were taken at different moments and for different purposes, and Scripture keeps both without harmonising them. The house of Azgad is a picture of a people slowly, unevenly, really coming back.
webster_summary: Head of a lay family of the return from Babylon, whose children came back in two companies and sealed Nehemiah's covenant.
webster_full: AZGAD, Hebrew Azgad, commonly read strong is Gad, or Gad is mighty.
The head of one of the families that returned from the Babylonian captivity.
A thousand two hundred twenty and two of his children returned with Zerubbabel.
Johanan the son of Hakkatan came up later with Ezra, and an hundred and ten males with him.
The house sealed the covenant in the days of Nehemiah.
scriptures: The children of Azgad, a thousand two hundred twenty and two.
The children of Azgad, two thousand three hundred twenty and two.
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
corruption_summary: Slow obedience is treated as no obedience; Scripture records the families who came home late alongside those who came home first.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No one disputes Azgad. What his record disputes is our impatience — with ourselves and with others — over the pace of obedience. The proclamation of Cyrus went out, the way home was open, and most of the exiles stayed in Babylon. Of the house of Azgad, twelve hundred came at once and a further hundred and ten came up with Ezra some sixty years later, one company under Johanan the son of Hakkatan. They came late. They came.

Scripture is honest about the mixture. The generation that laid the foundation wept and shouted at the same time, and the noise could not be told apart (Ezr 3:13). Restoration in the Bible is rarely a clean event; it is a long, partial, argued-over business in which some move early, some move late, and God is patient with both. The principle to recover is that the right response to a late return is to write the names down and get on with the building, not to rank the latecomers. He that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out (Joh 6:37) has no clause about timing.

etymology: Hebrew Adin (H5720), delicate, given to pleasure, voluptuous — from adan (H5727), to be soft or luxurious; the same root that gives Eden its name and gives the river of thy pleasures its word.
biblical_def: Adin is the head of a lay family of the return. Ezra's register counts the children of Adin, four hundred fifty and four (Ezr 2:15) and Nehemiah's six hundred fifty and five (Neh 7:20); Ebed the son of Jonathan came up later with Ezra bringing fifty males (Ezr 8:6); and the house sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:16). The name is the arresting thing. Adin means delicate or given to pleasure, from the root behind Eden and behind the psalmist's thou shalt make them drink of the river of thy pleasures (Psa 36:8). It is not a word Scripture treats as simply bad. Pleasure is God's invention: He planted a garden of delight and set man in it, and the promise at His right hand is pleasures for evermore (Psa 16:11). What Scripture condemns is not pleasure but pleasure detached from God and preferred to Him — lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God (2Ti 3:4), and the delicate man of Deuteronomy whose softness turns cruel under siege (Deu 28:54). That a family named delicate left the comforts of Babylon to rebuild a ruined city is its own small sermon.
webster_summary: Head of a lay family of the return from Babylon; the name means delicate, or given to pleasure.
webster_full: ADIN, Hebrew Adin, delicate, voluptuous, given to pleasure.
The head of one of the families that returned from the Babylonian captivity.
Four hundred fifty and four of his children returned with Zerubbabel.
Ebed the son of Jonathan came up later with Ezra, and fifty males with him.
The house sealed the covenant in the days of Nehemiah.
scriptures: The children of Adin, four hundred fifty and four.
Of the sons also of Adin; Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him fifty males.
The children of Adin, six hundred fifty and five.
corruption_summary: Pleasure is treated either as the highest good or as inherently suspect; Scripture makes it a good gift that becomes an idol when preferred to the Giver.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors stand opposite each other and the age commits both. The first makes pleasure the measure of a life — the assumption that what feels good is therefore good, and that any command restraining appetite is oppression. Paul named the type exactly: lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God (2Ti 3:4), and the comparative is the whole indictment. The sin is not that they loved pleasure; it is that they loved it more.

The second error is the ascetic reflex that treats enjoyment itself as worldliness, forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving (1Ti 4:3). Scripture will not have that either. He giveth us richly all things to enjoy (1Ti 6:17); the root of Adin's name is the root of Eden; and the endless prospect at God's right hand is pleasures for evermore. The principle to recover is the order: pleasure received from God's hand with thanksgiving is holy, and pleasure pursued as a substitute for God is the oldest idolatry there is.

etymology: Hebrew Neqoda (H5353), marked or distinguished — from naqod (H5348), speckled, marked with spots; the word used of Jacob's speckled flocks.
biblical_def: Nekoda names two groups in the registers of the return, and the second is the striking one. A family of Nekoda stands among the Nethinim, the temple servants (Ezr 2:48; Neh 7:50). But another company of the children of Nekoda appears in a different and poignant list: those who went up from Telmelah… but they could not shew their father's house, and their seed, whether they were of Israel (Ezr 2:59-60; Neh 7:61-62). They came home with everyone else, six hundred and fifty-two of them, and could not prove they belonged. The registers do not expel them and do not confirm them; they write the fact down and leave it standing. In the parallel case of the priests who could not find their register, the ruling was that they were put from the priesthood till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim (Ezr 2:63) — office suspended, the question referred to God. The name means marked, from the word for speckled flocks, and there is a quiet irony in it: a house called marked that could not produce its mark.
webster_summary: A name in the registers of the return: a family of the Nethinim, and a company who could not prove their Israelite descent.
webster_full: NEKODA, Hebrew Neqoda, marked, distinguished; from the word for speckled.
1. The head of a family of the Nethinim, the servants of the temple.
2. The head of a company who returned but could not shew their father's house.
Six hundred fifty and two came up who could not prove their seed, whether they were of Israel.
The priests in the same case were put from the priesthood until a priest should stand up with Urim and Thummim.
scriptures: The children of Rezin, the children of Nekoda, the children of Gazzam,
The children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda, six hundred fifty and two.
The children of Reaiah, the children of Rezin, the children of Nekoda,
The children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda, six hundred forty and two.
corruption_summary: Assurance is grounded in feeling or in mere profession; Scripture grounds it in evidence God Himself supplies, and is honest when the evidence is missing.
corruption_paragraphs: The children of Nekoda who could not shew their father's house are a standing rebuke to two opposite errors about assurance. The first is presumption — the assumption that anyone who walks in with the crowd belongs, that a profession made once settles the matter and no evidence need ever appear. The registers of Ezra and Nehemiah were kept precisely because Israel did not think that. Belonging was a matter of fact, and facts can be checked.

The second error is the despair that says no one can know. Scripture insists that assurance is available and commends the pursuit of it: These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life (1Jn 5:13), and give diligence to make your calling and election sure (2Pe 1:10). But the evidence is of a particular kind — the Spirit bearing witness with our spirit (Rom 8:16), and a changed life: we know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren (1Jn 3:14). The honest handling in Ezra 2, which neither expelled the doubtful nor pretended the question was settled, is the pastoral model: tell the truth about what is unproved, and refer the case to the Priest who is able to settle it.

etymology: Hebrew Giddel (H1435), very great or he has made great — from gadal (H1431), to grow, to become great, to magnify.
biblical_def: Giddel is the head of two families in the registers of the return — one among the Nethinim, the temple servants (Ezr 2:47; Neh 7:49), and one among the children of Solomon's servants (Ezr 2:56; Neh 7:58). Neither group had rank. The Nethinim were the given ones, assigned to the drudgery of the sanctuary: drawing water, cutting wood, carrying for the Levites. Solomon's servants were the descendants of labour gangs from the building of the first temple. They are listed at the very bottom of the register, after the priests, the Levites, the singers, the porters and the whole congregation of Israel — and they are listed. Their names are written in the same roll, by the same hand, with the same care. The name means very great, from gadal, the verb of magnifying: O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together (Psa 34:3). A man at the bottom of the register named very great is the kind of arrangement Scripture makes on purpose, since greatness in the kingdom is measured by the towel and the basin — whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister (Mat 20:26).
webster_summary: Head of two families of the return — one of the Nethinim, one of the children of Solomon's servants. The name means very great.
webster_full: GIDDEL, Hebrew Giddel, very great, or he has made great.
1. The head of a family of the Nethinim, the given ones who served the temple.
2. The head of a family of the children of Solomon's servants.
Both houses are named in the registers of Ezra and Nehemiah.
From gadal, to grow great, to magnify.
scriptures: The children of Giddel, the children of Gahar, the children of Reaiah,
The children of Jaalah, the children of Darkon, the children of Giddel,
The children of Hanan, the children of Giddel, the children of Gahar,
The children of Jaala, the children of Darkon, the children of Giddel,
corruption_summary: Greatness is measured by position and reach; Christ measures it by service, and Scripture writes the servants' names down.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Giddel is disputed by no one. What his placing in the register disputes is the instinct that ranks people by usefulness to the institution. The Nethinim and the children of Solomon's servants were the lowest orders of the restored community, doing the work nobody writes hymns about, and the inspired register spends its ink on their family names one by one.

The Lord Jesus settled the question of greatness in terms that have never been softened: whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister; and whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many (Mat 20:26-28). The measure is not scale but service, and the pattern is the Son of God with a towel. The principle to recover is that a man named very great at the bottom of the list is exactly where the Bible expects greatness to be found, and that the church which forgets this will keep promoting the wrong people.
